name: PT Segar Kumala Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Segar Kumala Indonesia — a thin-margin fruit distributor carried by a school-meals programme
frontmatter.summary: We initiate BUAH at REDUCE with a target of Rp356. The free-meals programme has lifted volumes, but the fourth quarter is seasonally thin, the FY2025 accounts show a Q4 gross margin far below the nine-month rate, and the shares trade at a large premium to retail peers. The dividend is real but the price already capitalises it; the peer multiple and the illiquidity discount leave no return.
thesis: MBG is real demand, not a story: the programme reached 57 million beneficiaries by September 2026 [S12], and its shift towards fruit lifted FY2025 revenue growth to 47.7% [S9].

The incremental business is thin and the fourth quarter is the weakest: FY2025 Q4 gross margin was far below the nine-month rate [S9][S10], and applying that actual Q4 pattern to the 9M2026 margin gives FY2026E gross margin of 6.6%, not the nine-month run-rate.
At 18.1x FY2025A earnings against a peer median of 9.1x, the shares discount a growth and margin profile the accounts do not show [S0].

Our DCF values the equity at Rp473 a share, only just above the price, and the peer‑multiple cross‑checks and the 20.0% illiquidity discount take the target to Rp356. The 4.9% yield does not cover the gap.
Related-party purchases of IDR617.2bn, around a fifth of all buying, and an 11.0% per cent free float against a fifteen per cent minimum are the governance items to watch [S9][S11].

catalysts.event: FY2026 results and declaration of the final dividend
Annual general meeting; dividend approval and any free-float plan
Gorontalo cold store opening; update on the Lampung ramp
MBG budget and beneficiary target for the following fiscal year

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Segar Kumala Indonesia (BUAH) with a **REDUCE** rating and a target of Rp356, -21.9% against the last price and -17.0% including the dividends we expect over the next twelve months. This is the revised initiation after the first red-team round. We have replaced the FY2026 gross-margin assumption with the company's actual fourth-quarter pattern, set the payout to the practised near-total distribution, and valued the shares on peer rather than post-IPO multiples; each change is sourced below, and together they remove the ADD. The company imports and distributes fresh fruit, mostly from China, through a network of cold stores that has grown from a single Jakarta operation into a national one [S4][S9]. Its moment arrived in the middle of 2025, when the government's free nutritious meals programme (MBG) replaced ultra-processed items with fruit; the company itself dates the sales effect to that decision [S11].

The result is a business that grew revenue 47.7% in FY2025 to IDR3,273.0bn [S9], and still managed IDR2,821.3bn of sales in the first nine months of 2026 [S10]. What did not grow was profit per rupiah of sales. Gross margin fell from 8.5% in FY2023 to 6.9% in FY2025, and net profit in the nine months to September 2026 was IDR45.0bn, below the same period a year earlier, because cost of goods and branch overheads grew faster than sales [S9][S10].

Our variant view is not that MBG is fake — it is that the market is paying a quality multiple for a volume contract. The shares trade on 20.2x our FY2026 earnings and 11.6x EV/EBITDA, against a peer median P/E of 9.1x [S0], for a distributor earning 1.5% net and buying around a fifth of its goods from related parties [S9]. Management's IDR80.0bn profit target for 2026, set at the May public expose, is out of reach on the current run-rate; we forecast IDR45.2bn [S11].

Three things move the value. First, the gross margin: gross profit of IDR224.4bn carries operating profit of IDR66.3bn, so a single point of margin is a large share of profit, and the fourth quarter is structurally the weakest — FY2025 Q4 gross profit of the year less the nine-month figure leaves a quarter at a margin far below the nine-month rate [S9][S10]. Second, MBG retention: the programme is a fiscal choice, and caterers can in principle buy directly. Third, the related-party supply chain: purchases of IDR617.2bn from common-control entities are the channel through which value can leave the listed company without appearing in its margin [S9].

The stock is illiquid — a three-month average daily traded value of IDR171.7m on a free float of 11 per cent [S11]. House policy applies a 20.0% discount to the fundamental value, and because the DCF is already only slightly above the last price, that discount is what takes the target below it. The 4.9% yield is real and near-total in payout terms, but on our corrected earnings it does not cover the downside. We would revisit if the fourth-quarter margin recovered to the nine-month rate, if the related-party supply terms were shown to be at arm's length, or if a free-float placement repriced the illiquidity discount; none of those is in the base case.

Segar Kumala was founded in 2017 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in August 2022 [S4]. It is, in substance, an import-and-distribute business: fruit is bought overseas — the company says 66.0% of its imported products come from China — landed, quality-checked at a distribution centre in Surabaya and moved through refrigerated branches to modern retail, traditional trade and, increasingly, institutional caterers [S11]. Frozen chicken is a small second line. In FY2025 fruit sales were IDR3,226.0bn against IDR65.6bn in chicken, with the balance of the gross figure being sales discounts [S9]. Volumes in FY2024, the last year the annual report quantifies them, were 119,109 tonnes tonnes of fruit and 1,211 tonnes tonnes of frozen chicken [S4].

The asset base is the cold chain, not the warehouse. At the end of 2024 the company operated 16.0 branches branches or cold stores with 8,305 tonnes tonnes of capacity after the Ternate and Jayapura openings in 2025 [S4][S7]. It added Lampung in 2026 and has Gorontalo under construction; the IDR12.0bn 2026 budget covers both branches alongside warehouse modernisation and refrigerated trucks, so it is a programme total, not a per-branch cost [S11]. The company does not disclose branch-level revenue, and we do not invent one: we treat the branch count as a capacity constraint on consolidated growth rather than a per-branch build-up. The four openings since the end-2024 base are a meaningful increase in distribution points, but the new branches are in smaller markets, and there is no disclosed revenue per branch to extrapolate [S4][S11]. The company employed 466 people people at the end of 2025, up from a smaller base the year before [S9] — the branch network, not head office, is where the cost sits.

Customers are fragmented. The FY2025 accounts state that no single customer accounted for more than a tenth of sales, and that is true of the prior year as well [S9]. That is a genuine strength in a business where a single lost account would otherwise be existential; it also means the company has little negotiating leverage over any one buyer. Related-party sales of IDR201.4bn in FY2025 [S9] are a meaningful slice of the customer base and are discussed in the governance section.

The controlling shareholder is the founding Susilo family. Hendro Susilo and Micheal Iksan Susilo between them hold the large majority of the shares, insiders own 88.8% in total, and the free float is 11 per cent on the company's own May‑2026 disclosure [S11][S4] — the data page's 12.2% is computed on a different share base, and we use the company figure throughout [S0]. Renny Lauren, the president director, is also a shareholder; Micheal Iksan Susilo chairs the board of commissioners and Hendro Susilo sits on it, with one independent commissioner [S9]. There is no second listed vehicle in the group, so the listed company is the operating business rather than a holding shell.

Competitively, BUAH is a challenger. The Indonesian fruit trade is fragmented between importers, wholesale markets and regional distributors [S11], and the listed company's advantage is logistical density — cold stores in secondary cities that a Jakarta-only importer cannot serve economically. That is the moat variable our method card names for Indonesian consumer names: distribution reach. It is a real but narrow advantage, because the cold store itself is replicable capital and the product is undifferentiated. Nothing in the accounts suggests pricing power: the gross margin has fallen as volumes grew [S9].

Fresh fruit is a perishable, seasonal and largely undifferentiated product. Importers compete on
landed cost, clearance speed and the ability to hold stock in cold chain without shrink, and buyers
can switch supplier between shipments. In most markets this produces structurally thin distributor
margins and returns that depend on turnover and working-capital terms rather than on brand. Scale
helps mainly through freight and storage utilisation, which is why branch density — not a brand —
is the usual source of advantage in this trade.

Strategy follows from that. The company adds one or two branches a year into cities where the nearest alternative is a wholesaler, and it follows institutional demand where a government programme creates a large, repeat, volume customer [S11][S12]. It does not advertise, does not own farms and does not manufacture. The main strategic question is whether the institutional volume leaves enough margin to pay for the branches it requires; the FY2025 and nine-month 2026 accounts suggest it does not, or not yet [S9][S10].

The demand driver that matters is MBG. The programme spent IDR153.19tn in the nine months to September 2026 and reached 57 million beneficiaries by then, according to the finance ministry [S12]; the nutrition agency reported the programme at a similar scale early in the year [S13]. For a distributor, that is a step-change in the addressable institutional market: meals are served daily, the produce basket is standardised, and the caterers who win the contracts need a supplier who can deliver in volume to many locations.

The composition of the meal matters as much as its size. BUAH's own account is that the government decided in the middle of 2025 that meals should not rely on ultra-processed food and should include fruit instead, and that this decision drove its sales [S11]. That is a policy-dependent demand curve, not a consumer trend. The programme is funded from the budget, administered by a dedicated agency, and can be re-scoped by regulation; the company's volume is therefore exposed to decisions it does not influence.

Supply is import-dependent and dollar-denominated. Around 66.0% of imported product comes from China, and the company describes rupiah fluctuation as having a material effect, with mitigation through currency diversification into renminbi [S11]. The actuals give the pass-through test: gross margin fell from 7.8% in FY2024 to 6.9% in FY2025 while the house deck's average rate moved from 15,846 to 16,448, and the nine-month 2026 margin held near the FY2025 level despite the deck's further move to 17,570. That is evidence of substantial, if lagged, pass-through rather than full absorption. Our base case holds the annual margin at 6.6% — below FY2025, so neither a recovery nor a further FX haircut is assumed — and the currency shock sits in the bear case. The deck's forward path to 18,350 is a drift, not a step; if it accelerates, the bear's margin shock is the right template.

Domestic competition comes from other importers and from the wholesale markets, and the listed peers in our coverage are retailers rather than distributors: Alfamart, Midi and DFI are customers of businesses like this, not competitors [S4][S9]. That matters for relative valuation — the peer multiples in the valuation section are retail multiples, and a distributor should not command them unless its returns are comparable, which at a 1.5% net margin they are not [S9].

Regulation cuts both ways. Import licensing and food-safety rules raise the cost of being an importer and favour established operators with cold chain; the same rules can be tightened with little notice. The exchange's free-float requirement is the other regulatory constraint: the company disclosed an 11.0% free float against a minimum that rises over time, with a deadline it described as running to 2029 [S11]. Any compliance route — a placement, a split of the family's holding, a secondary sell-down — adds supply.

We have not sourced a defensible estimate of the total Indonesian fruit-distribution market, and we do not manufacture one here. What can be said from the filings is that BUAH's revenue is a small fraction of a very large, fragmented trade, that its growth has come from adding geography and institutional volume rather than from taking share in existing cities, and that its margins are below what a retailer earns because it performs logistics rather than retail [S9][S10].

Five forces, briefly. Buyer power is high: customers are large retailers and institutional caterers with alternative suppliers, and no customer is above a tenth of sales only because the base is spread thin [S9]. Supplier power is high and complicated by related-party purchases of IDR617.2bn [S9]. New entrants face the cold-chain cost but not a licence moat, so entry is easy at small scale and hard at national scale. Substitutes are other proteins and other fruit sources. Rivalry is intense and expressed in price, which is why volume growth has not produced margin expansion.

Revenue has compounded quickly: IDR1,386.1bn in FY2022 to IDR1,783.3bn in FY2023, IDR2,215.6bn in FY2024 and IDR3,273.0bn in FY2025 [S4][S9]; the FY2022 and FY2023 figures come from the five-year summary in the FY2024 annual report, not the FY2025 accounts, which carry only two years. The acceleration in FY2025 (47.7%) coincides with the MBG change the company describes, and it continued into 2026, with IDR2,821.3bn of sales in the nine months to September against IDR3,273.0bn for the whole of the prior year [S10]. Growth of that kind in a distribution business is bought with working capital and branch cost, and the accounts show both.

Margins tell the other half of the story. Gross margin fell from 8.5% in FY2023 to 7.8% in FY2024 and 6.9% in FY2025, and we forecast 6.6% for FY2026, below the nine-month run-rate because the fourth quarter is seasonally the weakest [S9][S10]. SG&A and other operating costs were IDR157.6bn on IDR3,273.0bn of sales — around 5.0% of revenue, the level we hold in the forecast — as new branches carry start-up cost before they carry volume [S9]. The result is an EBIT margin of 2.0% and a net margin of 1.5%: a business where a small change in spread is a large change in profit.

The nine-month 2026 figures are the most important evidence in this report. Sales rose, gross profit rose, and net profit fell to IDR45.0bn from IDR49.4bn a year earlier, because cost of goods took a larger share of revenue and administrative costs grew faster than sales [S10]. That is the signature of a volume programme priced at thin spreads, not of operating leverage. The fourth quarter is the reconciliation that matters: FY2025 gross profit of IDR224.4bn against IDR177.9bn for the nine months to September 2025, on revenue of IDR3,273.0bn against IDR2,387.9bn, leaves a fourth quarter whose gross margin was far below the nine-month rate; EBIT of IDR66.3bn against IDR64.4bn over the same nine months completes the picture [S9][S10]. The cause is year-end discounting and the fruit-mix shift, both of which recur. We therefore do not carry the 9M2026 gross margin — gross profit IDR197.3bn on IDR2,821.3bn of sales [S10] — into the fourth quarter. We apply the actual Q4-2025 margin to Q4-2026 revenue, which gives FY2026E gross margin of 6.6%, EBIT of IDR58.4bn and net profit of IDR45.2bn. The gap against the nine-month run-rate is the Q4 step-up the earlier draft assumed without a source.

Cash conversion has been volatile but is not a red flag. In FY2025 operating cash flow of IDR83.8bn exceeded net profit of IDR50.4bn largely because trade payables grew, including IDR617.2bn of purchases from related parties [S9]. In FY2024 the reverse was true — operating cash flow of IDR3.3bn against net profit of IDR35.3bn — as working capital absorbed funds; FY2023 was in between, with operating cash flow of IDR32.2bn and net profit of IDR38.8bn [S5]. On total assets of IDR340.8bn, IDR394.1bn and IDR487.6bn for FY2023 to FY2025 [S4][S5][S9], the method card's accruals ratio runs at roughly two per cent in FY2023, close to a tenth of assets in FY2024 and negative in FY2025. The FY2024 figure is the payables squeeze, not earnings outrunning cash, and FY2025 more than reverses it. Receivables grew more slowly than sales in FY2025 [S9]. We treat the working-capital benefit as real but finite; our forecast assumes working capital settles at 1.2% of revenue, below the FY2025 level but not negative.

The balance sheet is conservative. There is no bank debt: total debt of IDR2.7bn is almost entirely lease liabilities, against cash of IDR104.2bn, so the company holds more cash than gross debt [S9]. Equity is IDR199.1bn, and return on equity was 25.9% in FY2025 — flattered by a small equity base and a near-total payout rather than by high margins [S9]. Capex was IDR17.5bn in FY2025 and management budgets IDR12.0bn for 2026, which operating cash flow can fund several times over [S9][S11].

Capital allocation is the family's dividend. The company declared IDR50.0bn for FY2025 in two tranches — the final IDR25.0bn approved at the May-2026 RUPS and the interim paid in November 2025 — which is essentially the whole of FY2025 net profit of IDR50.4bn [S9][S11]. The IDR46.0bn in the FY2025 cash-flow statement is cash paid, not the dividend declared on the year: it comprises the prior year's final and the FY2025 interim [S9]. The FY2026 interim of IDR20.0bn declared in October 2026 was almost the whole of IDR21.8bn of first-half net profit [S3]. The stated policy caps payout at a lower share of profit, so practice is far above policy [S4]. Our forecast uses the practised rate, 99.0%. That is good for income and bad for the equity buffer: with a thin margin and a growing branch network, a poor year would force either a dividend cut or new debt. Neither is in our base case, but both are live.

Our forecasts assume revenue growth of 10.0% in FY2027E, fading to 6.0% by FY2030E, gross margin of 6.6% and SG&A of 4.9% of sales, with the practised payout of 99.0% and terminal growth below long-run nominal GDP. The path is deliberately below the FY2025 step-up: the MBG base effect annualises and branch additions slow. We do not extrapolate the programme beyond the 57 million beneficiaries reached in September 2026, because the finance ministry publishes no forward beneficiary target and says the budget will adjust to need rather than to a fixed plan [S12]. The forecast also assumes no further related-party supply shock and no equity issuance for the free-float requirement in the base case [S9][S10][S11]; the placement is in the bear.

On the method card's remaining screens, receivables and inventory have not outgrown sales, there is no capitalised development cost, and related-party flows are disclosed rather than hidden [S9][S10]. The IDX board and notation status is a verification gap, not a clean bill: idx.co.id is outside our source registry, the filings do not state a special board, and the data page we cite shows ordinary trading [S8]. The exchange now displays a special notation P for issuers below its minimum free float, applied in stages from the current half-year [S16], which at a 11 per cent float would reach BUAH on the later timetable if it has not placed shares by then [S11]; we carry that and the FY2025 audit opinion as unverified limitations, set out in the governance section. The one confirmed structure flag is the concentration of purchases with common-control suppliers, quantified in the governance section [S9].

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the company is a cash‑generative distributor with a stable capital structure and a high payout, which is exactly the case a DCF handles well; we cross‑check with P/E and EV/EBITDA because a small, illiquid name can trade away from its fundamental value for long periods, and the market's multiple is information. Weights are those of the industry template: six parts DCF, three parts P/E, one part EV/EBITDA.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck: a rupiah risk‑free rate of 7.4%, a sovereign default spread of 1.6% subtracted from it, a mature‑market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and an unlevered beta of 0.70 from the industry default, relevered for a debt‑to‑equity ratio of 0.00. That gives a cost of equity of 11.0%: (7.4% − 1.6%) + 0.70 × (4.2% + 2.5%) + 0.5%.

The 0.5% premium we add is for small size, family control and related‑party supply concentration — IDR617.2bn of FY2025 purchases came from common‑control suppliers [S9] — not for illiquidity, which the traded‑value discount prices separately. The final WACC of 11.0% sits at the bottom of the house IDR band. Without the premium the build drops below the band, which would be too cheap for a majority‑controlled name with an 11 per cent public float [S11].

The DCF values the equity at Rp473 a share. The terminal value is 55.0% of the total, which is not unusual for a model with low capital intensity, but the multiple it implies is the test that matters. On FY2035E EBITDA of IDR125.4bn the terminal value is an exit multiple just under nine times — against a little under nine times the enterprise value a buyer pays today over FY2027E EBITDA and about ten times over FY2026E on the September‑2026 balance sheet. The engine's 11.6x is the FY2026E figure built on year‑end‑2026 net debt, not a trailing multiple; the same metric on today's net cash is ten and a half times. The exit multiple is therefore a mild contraction from today's, not an expansion, so the value does not depend on a large re‑rating. That is the method card's multiple‑survival test, and the model passes it. The DCF is also Rp473 against a Rp456 price — above it by a few per cent — so the cash‑flow method on its own does not support the sell; the target comes from the market‑based cross‑checks and the illiquidity discount.

The cross‑checks disagree, and the disagreement is the valuation. The P/E method gives Rp230, -51.5% below the DCF, on a multiple of 9.1x — the peer median for small Indonesian staple distributors [S0]. BUAH itself trades at 18.1x FY2025A earnings and 20.2x FY2026E, about twenty times on the last twelve months — roughly double that peer median and its own high of the last four years. The EV/EBITDA method gives Rp277 on 4.9x, against the 10.6x the shares carried on FY2025A EBITDA. Either the DCF's long‑run assumptions are too generous or the market's multiple is a small‑cap premium that will fade. We weight the DCF most, but the two market‑based methods pull the weighted value to Rp380, well below DCF value.

There is a second, larger haircut. House policy discounts the fundamental value of an illiquid stock by its liquidity band, and BUAH's traded value of IDR171.7m a day falls in the widest band, a 20.0% discount. That takes the scenario‑weighted value of Rp445 to the Rp356 target. In substance, the analysis says the business is worth around its price on cash flow, less than the market pays on multiples, and that a public‑market buyer cannot realise either gap without a control event or a much larger float.

Since the 30 September 2026 balance sheet we have checked the October 2026 interim dividend of IDR20.0bn [S3], the float plan [S11] and the Q3 LK [S10]. Neither is a separate bridge item: the interim dividend is already inside the FY2026E payout assumption and the share price is quoted after its declaration, and the float placement is modelled as the bear‑case share‑count shock. The bridge is deliberately empty rather than unreviewed [S3][S10][S11].

The sensitivity table shows how much rides on the discount rate and terminal growth, and on the two operating inputs that carry the thesis: revenue growth and gross margin. A one‑point change in gross margin is worth more to the value than a one‑point change in growth, because the margin flows straight to EBIT while growth needs working capital and branch cost. That is the right way to think about the risk: this is a spread business, and the spread is what we are underwriting.

The call is not a knife‑edge, but it is not comfortable either. The target sits a fifth below the price, so it would take a material gross‑margin recovery or a much higher traded‑value band to bring the shares back inside the HOLD range; the WACC row of the sensitivity table shows that a one‑point higher cost of capital takes the DCF down by about a tenth, and by about a seventh if terminal growth falls a point at the same time — either way it widens rather than closes the gap. On the other side, the DCF is only a few per cent above the price, so a peer multiple moving towards BUAH's own history would move the call the other way; we have tested that by doubling the bear probability and halving the base, and the weighted target falls further, so the conclusion survives the probability shift.

What does today's price imply? Run the model backwards and the current share price discounts revenue growth of 9.3% in FY2027E, indistinguishable from our 10.0% forecast. On the DCF alone the shares are close to fair value. The recommendation therefore does not rest on a cash‑flow shortfall: it rests on the multiple. A 11 per cent free float is being valued at 18.1x FY2025A earnings — 20.2x FY2026E, about twenty times on the last twelve months — for a thin‑margin distributor whose peer median is 9.1x, and the dividend yield of 5.5% on the declared FY2025 dividend is what a holder is actually paid while the re‑rating risk resolves [S11]. The rating is about the entry multiple and the illiquidity, not about a growth surprise.
The risk in this name is not demand in the abstract. It is the programme that creates the demand, the currency in which the product is bought, and the float in which the shares trade.

**Programme risk — likelihood medium, impact high.** The free-meals programme has reached 57 million beneficiaries and has spent IDR153.19tn to the end of September 2026 [S12]. BUAH has no contract with the programme; it sells into caterers who bid for it, and the government can re-scope the menu, change the procurement rules or slow the rollout at any budget cycle [S11][S12]. The step-up in FY2025 revenue is the programme annualising, not a contract backlog, and if the fruit component is reduced the volume base shrinks with it. We do not put a probability on a policy change, but we do not assume the programme grows beyond its current coverage either.

**Currency and spread risk — likelihood high, impact medium.** Around 66 per cent of imports come from China and the company describes rupiah movement as material, with partial natural hedging through renminbi purchases [S11]. The house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar by FY2027E; a weaker currency raises landed cost against sales priced in rupiah. Gross margin already fell from 8.5% in FY2023 to 6.9% in FY2025 as programme volume arrived at thin spreads [S9], and our forecast holds it near 6.6% rather than recovering [S10]. The risk is that it goes lower, not that we are assuming a recovery.

**Execution and cold-chain risk — likelihood medium, impact medium.** The asset base is 8,305 tonnes of cold storage across 16 branches [S4][S7], with Lampung opened and Gorontalo under construction in 2026 [S11]. Every new branch carries start-up cost before it carries volume, which is why SG&A rose as a share of sales in the first nine months of 2026 [S10]. A delayed branch or a cold-chain failure during a perishable shipment hits margin directly.

**Float and governance risk — likelihood medium, impact high.** The company disclosed a free float of 11 per cent against the exchange minimum, with a deadline running to 2029 and no plan yet [S11]. Closing a four‑point gap means placing roughly one share in twenty‑five of the existing count — the engine's bear case models a four‑point increase in shares — into a stock that trades IDR171.7m a day [S0]. A buyback is "still in planning" with no terms and would widen, not close, the gap, so we treat it as optionality, not as support [S11]. The same family controls the company and supplies IDR617.2bn of its purchases, a large share of the total [S9]; related‑party terms are disclosed but not negotiated at arm's length in any market sense, and the payables to those suppliers rose again in the first nine months of 2026 [S10].

The scenarios are mirrored on the three shared inputs — revenue growth, gross margin and working capital — moved by equal amounts in opposite directions, so neither case is a disguised haircut. The bear adds one non‑mirrored shock: the four‑point placement the free‑float rule requires, which is a regulatory obligation with a computable size rather than a view, and the bull has no matching issuance because no compliant route would shrink the share count [S11]. The bear also assumes the programme stops growing and the rupiah stays weak; the bull assumes coverage extends and the new branches mature quickly. Probabilities put half the weight on the base case, with the remainder split evenly between the tails. The weighted target sits above the base‑case target because the bull's upside is larger in percentage terms than the bear's loss.

Signposts that would change the view: - Nine-month gross margin below 6.6% with revenue still growing would confirm that programme volume is bought, not earned, and tilt probability toward the bear case. - A 2027–2028 school-year procurement round with a larger fruit component, or explicit programme expansion beyond the current beneficiary count, would tilt toward the bull case [S12]. - A placement or sell-down to meet the free-float rule would reset both the supply and the discount-rate premium; we would re-underwrite the target on the terms, not on the announcement. - A dividend cut, or a shift from near-total payout to funded capex, would remove the income support that carries much of the total return [S9][S11].

**Ownership and control.** The founding Susilo family — Micheal Iksan Susilo (president commissioner) and Hendro Susilo (commissioner) — controls the majority of the equity; together with other insiders they own 88.8% of the shares [S4][S9]. The free float is 11 per cent on the company's own disclosure, below the exchange's fifteen-percent minimum, and the company disclosed a deadline of 2029 to meet the rule without yet announcing a plan [S11]. There is no second listed vehicle in the group; the operating business is the listed company [S9].

**Related-party flows.** In FY2025 the company bought IDR617.2bn worth of goods from related parties, a large share of its total purchases [S9]. It sold IDR201.4bn to related parties, a smaller share of revenue [S9]. At September 2026 its trade payables to related parties stood at IDR201.7bn against IDR19.5bn of receivables from them [S10]; both rose during 2026, the payables far more than the receivables. The relation is supplier/customer. The LK includes the balance-sheet and income-statement disclosures required by PSAK 224, but not a statement of whether the terms are those of an arm's-length transaction, because the standard does not require one [S9].

**Board and audit.** The board of commissioners includes one independent commissioner, Bagus Abimanyu Lulu, and the board of directors comprises Renny Lauren (president director) and Vianita Januarini (director) [S9]. The FY2024 statements were audited by Tjahjadi & Tamara, Registered Public Accountants, with an unqualified opinion and a key audit matter on trade‑receivable impairment [S5]. The FY2025 filing is the audited set with the auditors' report bound into it, but the report pages did not survive our text extraction, so we treat the FY2025 opinion as unverified rather than assume the prior year's clean opinion carried over [S9].

**Verification gaps.** Two investability gates from the earnings-quality screen are open and stay open in this report. First, the FY2025 audit opinion: the audited filing [S9] is titled as audited and its table of contents lists the independent auditors' report, but the opinion pages did not survive text extraction and a targeted search found neither the "we have audited" wording nor a separately published signed opinion, so we do not infer that the FY2024 unqualified opinion carried over [S5][S9]. Second, the IDX board and notation status: idx.co.id is outside our source registry, so we checked the filings, which disclose no special board, the third-party data page we cite, which shows ordinary trading [S8], and the press for a notation announcement, which returned nothing specific to BUAH. What we can date is the regime: from 31 July 2026 the exchange displays a special notation P on the code of any issuer below its minimum free float, phased in for Acceleration Board issuers on 30 November 2026 and for Main and Development Board issuers on 30 April 2027, while notation letters E, D, A and S are removed as their criteria move into the Special Monitoring Board rules [S16]. At a 11 per cent float [S11] BUAH would expect notation P from the Main Board date if it has not placed shares by then; we carry it as expected rather than confirmed, and we found no indication that the shares sit on the Special Monitoring Board, though that is the same unverified exchange gate. Neither gap is a clean bill, and neither changes the rating on its own.

**Dividend practice vs. policy.** The company declared IDR50.0bn for FY2025 — a first tranche paid in November 2025 and the IDR25.0bn final approved at the May‑2026 RUPS — against net profit of IDR50.4bn [S9][S11]. That is essentially the whole year's profit and well above the payout cap in the annual report's policy; the company was in net cash at September 2026 with no bank debt, so the practice is affordable, but it leaves no retained‑earnings buffer for a thin‑margin year or unexpected capex [S4][S10]. The IDR46.0bn in the FY2025 cash‑flow statement is cash paid, not declared: it combines the FY2024 final with the FY2025 interim and should not be divided by FY2025 profit [S9]. The FY2026 interim of IDR20.0bn was declared in October 2026 against 1H2026 profit of IDR21.8bn [S3], so the near‑total payout is continuing into the current year.

**ESG exposures.** The business has a single operational material exposure: the carbon footprint and logistics footprint of imported products, including air-freighted fresh fruit. No sustainability report is filed; the annual report includes a page on green and social initiatives, but not a quantified performance section [S4]. Perishable-food safety is the primary operational-risk category, followed by employee health and safety (466 employees [S9]) and data privacy for its customer database; none of these have resulted in a disclosed material incident in the filings we read.

In Indonesia, related-party transactions between a controlling family's supply business and the listed
distribution vehicle are common and are expected to be fully disclosed under the related-party disclosure standard. The risk is
not that they exist — it is that they can increase without a clear business rationale or price
comparability disclosure, transferring margin from the listed entity to the unlisted supplier.
Dividend policies that separate practice from written policy are also common, often to the
shareholders' immediate benefit and the company's long‑term cost. Cold‑chain logistics for perishables
imposes food‑safety and waste‑reduction obligations that can become regulatory or reputational costs
if mismanaged.
The catalysts fall into scheduled financial announcements and programme cues.

**Financial announcements:** - March 2027: **FY2026 full-year results and dividend declaration** [S9]. The shares have moved on these each year, and the dividend is integral to the return. - May 2027: **Annual report publication** [S11]. The AR carries governance disclosures, notably the family's supply position. - First half 2027: **Public expose following the annual general meeting** [S11]. This is the platform for management to present progress on the free‑float plan and on programme participation. - During 2027: **Any placement or sell‑down to raise the free float to the exchange minimum** [S11]. An announcement would reset the supply side of the price — the exchange has enforced thresholds and the deadline runs to 2029.

**Programme cues:** - First‑half 2027: **School‑year 2027‑2028 MBG procurement round announcements** [S12]. The meal composition and volume targets shape institutional demand. - Mid‑2027: **National budget revisions and the school‑year procurement calendar** [S12]. A shift in education spending would matter only if it changes fruit's share of the meal.

**KPIs we watch between updates:** - **Gross margin** quarterly against our 6.6% forecast — the most‑likely reason for a surprise. - **Trade payables to related parties** as a share of total payables — the sign of a renegotiate. - **Branch openings** (after Lampung and Gorontalo) against the IDR12.0bn capex budget [S11]. - **Free‑float plan** announcements from the company or the exchange. - **Programme beneficiary count** against the 57 million baseline [S12]. - **USD/IDR** against the house macro deck — the largest cost driver.

Watchers should watch the cash rather than the revenue. The thesis rests on a thin‑margin distributor that returns cash, not on a growth‑plus‑margin expansion story; a widening between the payout policy and practice would be the first sign the cash is intended for something else [S9][S11].

bear.narrative: MBG volumes are cut or shift to caterers' own sourcing, no further branches open, and a weaker rupiah plus price competition squeeze gross margin. The 15% free-float rule forces a placement of roughly the four points of float the company lacks, adding supply at a discount [S11], and related-party suppliers tighten terms, pulling working capital back from its current negative level.

bull.narrative: MBG coverage extends beyond 57m beneficiaries, Lampung and Gorontalo mature quickly, and imported fruit costs ease with a stronger rupiah, lifting volumes and spreads together. Related-party suppliers extend terms further, releasing working capital. A buyback is in planning but has no disclosed terms and would widen rather than close the free-float gap, so it is not a value driver here [S11].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the 9M2026 actual (Rp2,821bn, +18.1% yoy [S10]) plus a Q4 at a normal branch run-rate, giving ~15% for the year and deliberately below management's May-2026 plan because the 2026 profit target of Rp80bn is already out of reach (9M2026 net profit Rp45.0bn [S10][S11]). Growth then fades to 10/8/7/6% as the MBG step-up annualises (57m beneficiaries to Sep-2026 [S12]) and branch openings slow to one or two a year (Lampung open, Gorontalo in build [S11]); long-run 4.5% is below IDR nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The fourth quarter is seasonally the weakest: FY2025 Q4 gross margin was 5.25% (FY2025 gross profit Rp224.4bn less 9M2025 Rp177.9bn on Q4 revenue Rp885.1bn) against 7.45% in 9M2025, and the year-end discounting that causes it recurs [S9][S10]. 9M2026 gross margin was 6.99% (gross profit Rp197.3bn on Rp2,821.3bn [S10]); holding that nine-month run-rate and repeating the actual Q4-2025 margin gives a full-year margin of 6.55%, which is what we model from FY2026E. No recovery towards the 2022-23 8.6% is assumed. The FY2026E figure is therefore not a haircut below the last actual but the last actual's own quarterly pattern applied to the 9M2026 rate.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 SG&A and other operating expense was 4.98% of sales (selling 0.75%, G&A 4.08%, other 0.15% [S10]) versus 4.82% in FY2025 [S9], as two branches (Lampung, Gorontalo) carry start-up cost. We model 5.0% in FY2026 easing to 4.9% as branches mature — no operating-leverage heroics.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A of Rp10.0bn (fixed-asset depreciation Rp6.92bn plus right-of-use depreciation Rp3.11bn [S9]) is 0.31% of revenue; capex slightly exceeds D&A so we drift the ratio to 0.33%.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management budgets Rp12bn of capex for 2026 (two branches, warehouse modernisation and refrigerated trucks [S11]); FY2025 cash capex was Rp17.5bn including right-of-use assets [S9]. We model 0.40% of revenue (~Rp15bn) falling to 0.35% — cold stores are the only real asset base.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 1.45% of revenue, and at 30 September 2026 it was negative (Rp-21.4bn) as trade payables, including Rp201.7bn to related suppliers at September 2026 [S9][S10], funded the MBG ramp. We assume 1.2% — below FY2025 because the payables extension is real, but not negative because it cannot keep stretching.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of Rp16.80bn on PBT of Rp67.16bn is a 25.0% effective rate [S9]; 9M2026 is 22.7% of PBT but we use the audited full-year rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The only borrowings are lease liabilities (Rp2.7bn at end-2025 [S9]); FY2025 lease interest of Rp250.7m implies ~9% and the balance is immaterial to value.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income of Rp1.13bn on opening cash of Rp85.3bn is only 1.3% [S9], but the cash balance has since grown to Rp181.3bn [S10] and BI-rate deposits now earn more; we use 2.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No bank debt and no issuance planned; new branches are funded from operating cash flow [S11].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating income; FY2025 contained a Rp1.8bn other operating charge.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests in the balance sheet or income statement [S9].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Practice, not the AR's 60% policy cap, is the anchor [S4]. For FY2025 the company declared Rp50bn in total (Rp25/share), 99.3% of the Rp50.36bn net profit: a Rp25bn interim paid in November 2025 and a further Rp25bn approved at the May-2026 RUPS [S9][S11]. The FY2026 interim declared in October 2026 was Rp20bn, 91.74% of 1H2026 net profit [S3]. We use 99% forward, the full-year FY2025 practice; the company has Rp179.7bn of net cash and no bank debt, so the Rp12bn branch capex budget and a near-total payout are not in conflict [S10].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issuance planned; the 2-for-1 split of October 2025 left the share count at 2,000m [S9]. The free-float rule (11% vs a 15% minimum by 2029 [S11]) could require a placement, but no terms are disclosed so it is not in the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% is below long-run IDR nominal GDP (house macro deck: CPI 3.28% plus real growth), appropriate for a mature, thin-margin distributor with no pricing power; the cap is 5.0%.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E is not built on the last actual. The model's FY2026E EBIT of Rp71.6bn requires Q4-2026 EBIT of Rp14.8bn against Rp1.9bn in Q4-2025 (FY2025 EBIT Rp66.3bn less 9M2025 Rp64.4bn [S9][S10]); its implied Q4 gross margin is 6.6% against 5.25% in Q4-2025 (FY2025 GP Rp224.4bn less 9M2025 Rp177.9bn on Rp885.1bn of Q4 revenue). The report itself says 'the fourth quarter carries the usual year-end discounts' yet models a +1.4pp Q4 margin swing with no source. Repeating the actual Q4 pattern gives FY2026 gross margin 6.55% and EBIT ~Rp58.7bn; on the report's own sensitivity a 0.25pp margin miss takes the target to ~Rp447, below the Rp456 price.
challenges.answer: Re-forecast on the actual Q4-2025 pattern: Q4 gross margin 5.25% (FY2025 GP 224.4 less 9M2025 177.9 on Q4 revenue 885.1) is applied to the 9M2026 rate, giving 6.55% for FY2026E and every forecast year. FY2026E EBIT is now 58.4 and net profit 45.2; the DCF falls to 473 from 584.

challenges.challenge: The two cross-checks are not peer cross-checks. The engine's P/E multiple of 16.74x is the average of a 9.12x peer median (AMRT 11.5x, HERO 8.6x, MIDI 9.1x, DMND 9.1x, EPMT 7.3x, DAYA 27.0x) and BUAH's own four-year mean of 24.36x - not the 'around 18.1x' own average the report cites, which is the current trailing multiple. Replacing both cross-checks with peer medians (P/E 9.12x -> Rp319; EV/EBITDA ~4.6x -> Rp271) gives a 60/30/10 blend of ~Rp473, a target of ~Rp401 and a total return of about -7%, i.e. HOLD. The report simultaneously argues peers trade at 'roughly half those levels'.
challenges.answer: Cross-checks are now pure peer medians (`multiple_source: peer_median`): P/E 9.1x gives 230 and EV/EBITDA 4.9x gives 277, against BUAH's 18.1x trailing multiple. The own-history mean of 24.4x is disclosed and not used; the weighted value falls to 380 and the target to 356.

challenges.challenge: Dividend facts are inconsistent in three places. The model carries FY2025 DPS Rp22.50 (Rp45bn, 89% payout); the report says 'the FY2025 dividend of IDR46.0bn was 89.4% of net profit'; the assumptions basis says 'FY2025 dividends of Rp50bn were 99% of net profit'. S9 shows the Rp46bn declared in 2025 is the FY2024 dividend (statement of changes in equity; Rp46bn is 130% of FY2024 profit of Rp35.3bn), while S11 states the FY2025 dividend is Rp50bn with a further Rp25bn (Rp12.5/share) declared at the May-2026 RUPS - i.e. Rp25/share and 99.3% of FY2025 net profit.
challenges.answer: Reconciles to the filings: FY2025 declared 50 (25 interim paid Nov-2025 plus 25 final approved May-2026), DPS 25, 99.3% of profit [S9][S11]. The 46 in the equity movement is cash paid (FY2024 final 21 plus FY2025 interim 25), not a 46 FY2024 dividend; the 130%-of-FY2024-profit claim is therefore wrong, though our 50/99.3% conclusion stands.

challenges.challenge: The 85% forward payout is an unsourced haircut below documented practice: FY2025 was 99.3% [S11] and the 1H2026 interim was ~92% on the report's own basis. At 99% the FY2026 DPS would be ~Rp27.3 against the model's Rp23.42, adding ~0.9pp to total return. In a call that clears the 10% ADD floor by 0.73pp that is rating-relevant, not a rounding.
challenges.answer: Payout raised from 85% to the practised 99% in every forecast year and terminal; FY2025 was 99.3% [S11] and the FY2026 interim was declared against 1H2026 profit at the same near-total rate [S3]. The higher DPS adds to the total return but does not change the REDUCE.

challenges.challenge: Cost of equity is set to the band floor and the disclosed build does not reconcile. The report quotes 7.4% risk-free + 4.2% ERP + 2.5% CRP at beta 0.70 + 0.5% premium, which gives ~12.6%, not 11.0%; the engine actually subtracts a 1.62pp sovereign default spread (COE = (7.45-1.62) + 0.70 x (4.23+2.46) + 0.50), which is not disclosed. Separately, the 50bp premium is justified partly by 'small size' and an 11-12% float - the same illiquidity the 20% target haircut prices, contrary to fund record's 'shown as its own line, never a hidden WACC premium'. A 12.0% WACC, still inside the 11-13% band, gives a DCF of Rp523 and a target of ~Rp413 (total return ~-4%).
challenges.answer: Full build disclosed: COE = (7.45 - 1.62) + 0.70 x (4.23 + 2.46) + 0.50 = 11.0%, including the 1.62pp sovereign default spread previously omitted. The 50bp premium is re-based on control and related-party concentration only; illiquidity is the separate 20% traded-value discount [S9].

challenges.challenge: Free-float compliance is disclosed but unpriced. The float is 11% [S11] (12.2% in the text [S0]; 88.8% insider ownership implies 11.2%) against a 15% minimum and a 2029 deadline. Closing the 4pp gap is 80m shares, Rp36.5bn at Rp456, or ~212 days of the Rp171.7m ADV; a placement would need a discount and would depress the very price the 20% liquidity haircut is meant to capture. Neither the base, the bear nor the liquidity discount reflects it, and 'no terms disclosed' answers a different question from 'no supply risk'.
challenges.answer: Float reconciled at 11% [S11] and the 4pp gap priced: the bear now includes a +4pp share-count shock, roughly 80m shares or 212 days of ADV at the current price [S0]. The 20% liquidity band is set by traded value, not float, so it survives a placement to 15%.

challenges.challenge: The ADD sits inside the model's own error bars and the report does not say so. It clears the 10% floor by 0.73pp; the engine's sensitivity shows 1pp of gross margin = Rp154/share pre-discount, so a 0.25pp miss takes the target to ~Rp447; ADV below Rp100m moves the haircut to 30% and the target to ~Rp421 (total return -2.5%); a 12% WACC gives ~Rp413. The prose presents a dividend story with 5.6% price upside but never tells the reader which input flips the rating to HOLD.
challenges.answer: Break-evens now stated in section 4: a quarter-point margin miss, a mid-band WACC or a 30% traded-value band all move the target further from the price, and doubling the bear probability lowers the weighted target again. The rating is REDUCE, so the test is what returns it to HOLD, not what held the old ADD.

challenges.challenge: FX is graded 'likelihood high' yet is absent from the base case. 66% of imports come from China and the company says rupiah moves have a strong impact [S11]; the house deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 by FY2027E (spot 18,012). The report says pass-through is 'partial and lagged' but holds gross margin at 6.9-7.0% for ten years, with the currency hit appearing only in the bear's -1.2pp margin shock. The deck's central FX path is not run through the imported cost base.
challenges.answer: Pass-through is evidenced rather than assumed: gross margin fell from 7.8% in FY2024 to 6.86% in FY2025 while USD/IDR moved from 15,846 to 16,448, and 9M2026 held 6.99% despite the deck's higher FY2026E rate [S9][S10]. The base no longer holds 6.9-7.0%: it holds 6.55%, the last actual's own quarterly pattern, with the FX shock in the bear.

challenges.challenge: Related-party economics are disclosed but not stress-tested. Purchases from common-control entities were Rp617.2bn, 20.5% of purchases [S9], with payables to them of Rp201.7bn at Sep-2026 against Rp124.5bn at Dec-2025 [S10] - the balance that produces the negative working capital - and no arm's-length statement. One point of margin on those purchases is Rp6.2bn, 12% of net profit, and the terms can be tightened at will; the bear case shocks only revenue, gross margin and opex.
challenges.answer: Related-party terms are now stressed through a +2pp working-capital shock in the bear, on top of the gross-margin shock that carries supplier pricing; the payables withdrawal is the mechanism that removes the negative working capital. The 617.2 of related purchases at one point of margin is roughly a tenth of net profit [S9][S10].

challenges.challenge: Two sourced upside items are missing. S11 says a share buyback is 'masih dalam perencanaan'; with Rp179.7bn net cash (19.7% of the Rp912bn market cap) and no bank debt, a buyback at 8.75x FY2026E EV/EBITDA would be materially accretive. And the base case caps MBG at the 57m beneficiaries reached by Sep-2026 [S12] and fades growth to 4.5% by FY2031 without sourcing the programme's forward budget or target; four branches added since 2025 are ~25% more distribution points than the 16 at end-2024 [S4][S7][S11] but no per-branch revenue is modelled.
challenges.answer: Buyback added to the bull narrative as optionality with no size, because S11 says only that it is "masih dalam perencanaan" with no terms and it would widen the float gap [S11]. The MBG cap is sourced: the finance ministry publishes no forward beneficiary target and says the budget adjusts to need [S12]. Per-branch revenue is dropped (not disclosed); branch count is a capacity constraint.

challenges.challenge: The auditor gap is real, but the report's inference is not neutral. The archived S9 contains the cover and contents naming an independent auditors' report but not the report itself, so the firm, opinion and any emphasis of matter are unknown; the report nonetheless asserts 'the filing is the audited set' and builds on it. With 20.5% related-party purchases and Rp350.7bn of trade payables, the opinion and key audit matters are load-bearing for an initiation.
challenges.answer: Auditor disclosed from the FY2024 set: Tjahjadi & Tamara, unqualified opinion, key audit matter on trade-receivable impairment [S5]. The FY2025 report pages did not survive extraction, so the FY2025 opinion is expressly stated as unverified rather than assumed clean [S9].

challenges.challenge: Two citation/reading errors. The FY2022 revenue of Rp1,386.1bn, FY2023 revenue of Rp1,783.3bn and the FY2023 gross margin of 8.5% are attributed to S9, but the FY2025 LK carries only 2025 and 2024; those figures are in the AR2024 five-year summary (S4 p.10: gross profit Rp152.4bn on Rp1,783.3bn). And the report says 'each new branch costing roughly IDR12.0bn' [S11], but S11 says Rp12bn is the total 2026 budget for two branches (Lampung and Gorontalo), not per branch.
challenges.answer: Citations corrected: FY2022/FY2023 revenue and the FY2023 margin are from the AR2024 five-year summary [S4], not the FY2025 LK. The capex sentence now says 12 is the total 2026 programme budget for two branches plus warehouse and truck spend, not a per-branch cost [S11].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is run across inconsistent periods. The report compares the implied exit multiple with the trailing 9.6x (FY2025A EBITDA), but the DCF's own first forecast year trades at 8.75x (EV Rp732bn / FY2026E EBITDA Rp83.7bn), and the terminal value of Rp1,411bn on FY2035 EBITDA of Rp153.8bn is 9.17x - about 5% multiple expansion on the forward measure, not contraction. The conclusion may still hold; the arithmetic as stated does not.
challenges.answer: Test restated like-for-like on the forward basis: the terminal value implies an exit multiple just under nine times FY2035E EBITDA against the roughly nine times forward multiple of the first forecast year and 11.5x trailing today, so the expansion is a few per cent, not contraction; the 55% terminal share is discussed in the same paragraph.

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality screens are asserted without numbers. The report says accruals 'swung with the payables cycle' but gives no ratio; from S9, FY2024 CFO was Rp3.34bn against Rp35.28bn net profit (about +9% of assets, near the 10% flag) and FY2025 was Rp83.77bn against Rp50.36bn. The IDX board/notation status is also asserted ('no special notation that we could find') with no exchange source cited, which the method card requires first.
challenges.answer: Accruals ratios are shown numerically from the filings (FY2023 CFO 32.2 vs NP 38.8; FY2024 CFO 3.3 vs NP 35.3 on average assets; FY2025 CFO 83.8 vs NP 50.4) and the FY2024 flag is explained as the payables squeeze [S5][S9]. The IDX board/notation status is now disclosed as unverified: idx.co.id is outside the source registry and the filings state no special board.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 closes with a dividend yield of 0.0%, but the model's FY2025A yield is 4.93% (DPS Rp22.50 on Rp456) and 5.5% on the declared Rp25.00; the template applies the pctv filter to a fractional field. The yield is the stated income support for holding through a re-rating.
challenges.answer: Yield now renders on the declared FY2025 DPS of Rp25.00 (Rp50bn on 2,000m shares), so the trailing yield is 5.5% not 0.0%; fact F49 restates the model series and the filter is pct on a fractional field [S11].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival paragraph is inverted: terminal value Rp1,094.6bn on FY2035E EBITDA Rp125.4bn is 8.73x against 8.96x on FY2027E (EV Rp732bn / EBITDA Rp81.7bn) and 10.4x on FY2026E, i.e. mild contraction; the text calls it mild expansion. The next sentence also says the DCF is a few per cent below the price when Rp473 is above Rp456.
challenges.answer: Multiple-survival test restated like-for-like: exit 8.7x FY2035E versus about 9.0x today EV over FY2027E and 10.4x FY2026E on the Sep-2026 balance sheet, i.e. mild contraction; the DCF of Rp473 is above the Rp456 price [S0][S9].

challenges.challenge: The WACC statement says a mid-band cost of capital lowers the DCF by roughly a quarter; the published sensitivity grid shows +1pp WACC (11.0% to 12.0%) taking Rp472.8 to Rp425.7, minus 10%, and only +2pp approaches minus 20%.
challenges.answer: WACC step corrected to the grid: +1pp WACC is -10% (Rp472.8 to Rp425.7); -14% is the corner with terminal growth also -1pp. The text now carries both magnitudes [S0].

challenges.challenge: Free float is 11% in S11 and in the bear-case placement sizing (4pp gap to the 15% minimum, 80m shares) but 12.2% in the summary, section 1 and section 6; the share shock and the illiquidity band are sized off different figures.
challenges.answer: Free float is 11% from the May-2026 public expose throughout the summary and sections 1, 4, 5 and 6; the 12.2% data-page figure is reconciled once as a different share base, and the 80m-share placement is sized off 11% [S11][S0].

challenges.challenge: fund record has no valuation.post_bs_review block and an empty valuation.bridge, although the method card requires a note and sources on what was searched since the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet date; the Rp20bn October-2026 interim dividend [S3] and the float plan are the obvious post-balance-sheet items.
challenges.answer: Added valuation.post_bs_review with sources and a section 4 paragraph: the Oct-2026 interim dividend of Rp20bn is inside the FY2026E payout and the post-declaration price, the float plan is the bear share shock, and no other post-balance-sheet event exists; the empty bridge is deliberate [S3][S10][S11].

challenges.challenge: The FY2025 audit opinion is disclosed as unverified, but the IDX board and notation status is not addressed at all; the earnings-quality card makes special-monitoring-board status and notation letters a first-order investability gate, and neither item was verified for this initiation.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now states both gates as limitations: the FY2025 opinion is unverified (auditors report pages missing, no signed opinion found) and the IDX board/notation status is unverified, with the notation P rule and its staged dates sourced to S16; no clean bill is inferred [S9][S8][S16].

challenges.challenge: The report calls 18.1x LTM earnings, but 18.1x is FY2025A net profit (Rp50.4bn); LTM net profit is Rp46.0bn, or 19.8x, and the summary's 20.2x is FY2026E. The central claim of a roughly 2x peer-median multiple is therefore period-ambiguous.
challenges.answer: Every multiple is period-labelled: 18.1x FY2025A, 20.2x FY2026E and about 19.8x on the last twelve months; the thesis, section 4 cross-checks and the implied-value paragraph no longer call FY2025A earnings LTM [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Omitted: the buyback management says is in planning [S11], with Rp179.7bn net cash (19.7% of market cap); branch additions (Ternate, Jayapura, Lampung, Gorontalo = +25% distribution points vs 16 at end-2024) with no modelled revenue; and any MBG expansion beyond the 57m already reached. The bull only shocks revenue +4pp and margin +1.2pp.

missing_bear_case.note: Omitted: the 15% free-float placement by 2029 (80m shares = Rp36.5bn = ~212 days of ADV); withdrawal of Rp201.7bn related-party payables that fund negative working capital; related-party margin extraction on 20.5% of purchases; and the FX path the report itself grades high-likelihood.

assumption_realism.note: The FY2026 build contradicts the last actual: Q4-2025 gross margin was 5.25% and Q4 EBIT Rp1.9bn, but FY2026E implies Q4 gross margin 6.6% and EBIT Rp14.8bn with no source. Gross margin also sits at 6.9% for ten years against 8.5% in FY2023 and 6.86% in FY2025.

evidence_and_citations.note: Auditor firm and opinion absent though the LK is audited and the archived text genuinely lacks the report page; FY2022-23 figures cited to S9 are in AR2024 (S4 p.10); dividend facts appear as Rp46bn, Rp45bn and Rp50bn in three places; 'each new branch costs Rp12bn' misreads S11's Rp12bn total two-branch budget.

valuation_method_fit.note: The P/E (16.74x) and EV/EBITDA (9.55x) cross-checks average peer medians of 9.12x and ~4.6-4.9x with BUAH's own four-year means of 24.36x and 14.19x; the report misstates the own average as 18.1x (the current trailing). Peer-only values (Rp319/Rp271) take the target to ~Rp401 and the rating to HOLD.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose argues the market overpays a 'volume contract' yet the ADD depends on own-history multiples and a band-floor WACC; a 0.25pp gross-margin miss, a 12% WACC or ADV below Rp100m each flips it to HOLD, which is not disclosed. The 5.6% price gap is inside the spread.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The macro deck is read only for the discount rate. USD/IDR FY2027E 18,350 (spot 18,012) is not run through the cost base even though 66% of imports are Chinese and the cost currency is USD/RMB; gross margin is held flat, so the deck's FX path has no effect on the base case.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: payout 85% vs 99.3% paid on FY2025 [S11]; terminal growth 4% justified only as 'below nominal GDP'; MBG capped at current coverage; Q4 revenue grown at 7% vs the 9M2026 run-rate of 18%. Unjustified optimism: the Q4 margin and own-history multiple anchors. The payout and Q4 items together move total return.

calibration.note: The engine's calibration gate passes (FY2025 EBITDA margin 2.33% actual vs 2.22% model, gap -0.11pp) and no BLOCK flags remain. The substantive margin problem is the FY2026 Q4 build, filed under assumption_realism (C1), not a gate failure.

findings.finding: Historical DPS line is one year late: model FY2024A DPS is Rp11.5, the FY2023 dividend (Rp23bn at Rp23/share pre-split, AR2024 [S4]); the FY2024 dividend approved 2 May 2025 was Rp21bn, Rp10.5 post-split [S6]. FY2022 7.0, FY2023 11.5, FY2025 25.0 are correct and the 46bn FY2025 cash paid reconciles as 21+25. No effect on forecast DPS, yield or target.

The model net_debt line is not re-based to the 30-Sep-2026 balance sheet (FY2026E -96.1 versus actual -179.7 [S10]) because NWC is assumed back to +1.2% of sales in Q4. The valuation correctly uses the actual -179.7 in the bridge and DCF, and section 4 discloses both EV/EBITDA bases, so value is unaffected; only the displayed cash line and the 11.6x cross-check rest on the projected figure.

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only ['a.share_change'], bull only [])
flags.justification: The bear-only a.share_change is the 4pp free-float placement required by the exchange's 15% minimum, a regulatory obligation with a computable size (80m shares to move 11% to 15%) [S11]. The bull has no share-count shock because the buyback is only "masih dalam perencanaan" with no disclosed terms and would widen, not close, the float gap [S11].
